scenario: AITA for “banning” my husband from the kitchen until he learns to respect my equipment? | I love to cook, I’ve been cooking since I was a little kid. I have some good cooking equipment that reflects that fact. My husband decided that he was going to start cooking as well, which I was all for. But he started cooking in the kitchen and damaging my equipment. A non-comprehensive list: * He cooks with my all-clad skillets with the heat up high for fifteen minutes, and then “washes” them by bringing them over to the sink and dousing them with cold water. He says he “likes the sizzle.” At least one of the skillets is warping a bit, it won’t sit straight on the stove anymore and doesn’t cook evenly. * He uses my chef’s knife to scrape crud off the counter. I told him to use my razor blade scraper to do it, he said “well, that would be overkill.” * I have a small toaster oven that acts as a mini-oven, I absolutely love. He butters toast BEFORE putting it in the oven. The fat drips onto the element. He did this so much that I’ve already had to have the element replaced once. He continues to do it and says “we can just replace it again.” * He cooked a tomato sauce in my seasoned cast iron skillet and then ran it through the dishwasher. * He leaves lemon juice, tomato, vinegar spills all over the granite countertops. When I tell him to clean up immediately, he laughs and says, “it’s granite, it’s indestructible!” This all annoyed me so much. I’m annoyed just typing it. Finally I told him that unless he starts actually respecting my equipment, I’m going to put it all under lock and key. He said, “what, you’re banishing me from the kitchen? From my own house?” I said “yes, you’re ruining all of my things.” He implied that it all belonged to him since he “bought it,” but I am fully aware that I had all of this stuff and bought all of this stuff before we got married. AITA? All I want is for him to respect my things. He knows that I hate when he does this stuff but he shouts and yells and calls me over critical every time I try to explain it to him. I’m at my wit’s end.

prediction.raw: I’ll answer this from a perspective of **fairness, communication, and mutual respect**—not as a personal judgment, but as a framework for evaluating the situation. Here’s my assessment: **Answer: 1 (AITF, but with caveats).** ### **Why?** 1. **Your Equipment is Yours (Legally and Emotionally):** - Even if he contributed financially to the household, the kitchen tools are *your* property (unless you explicitly shared ownership, which you haven’t). You have every right to protect them, especially since they’re irreplaceable (e.g., All-Clad, cast iron, granite countertops). His claim that "it belongs to him" is incorrect unless you’ve agreed otherwise. 2. **The Damage is Real and Irreversible:** - Warping pans, ruining countertops, and damaging a toaster oven element are not minor annoyances—they’re **financial and emotional losses**. Your frustration is valid. If he treated his own tools this way, you’d likely feel the same. 3. **His Dismissive Attitude is Unreasonable:** - His reactions ("it’s granite," "we can replace it," "overkill") show a lack of accountability. A partner who respects shared spaces (even if they’re primarily yours) would at least *try* to accommodate your needs. His yelling and defensiveness suggest he’s either: - **Ignorant** (doesn’t realize how much these things cost/maintain). - **Entitled** (believes rules don’t apply to him). - **Resentful** (may feel like you’re "controlling" him, which could be a deeper issue). 4. **The "Ban" is a Last Resort—but a Fair One:** - You’ve tried **education** (explaining care), **direct requests** (telling him to clean up), and **humor** (jokes about "overkill"). If he still refuses, **physical separation** (locking up tools) is a reasonable escalation. It’s not cruel—it’s **protecting your investment and sanity**. - *But:* This should be a **temporary** measure until he proves he’ll change. If he’s truly committed to cooking, he should: - Use **his own** basic tools (a cheap pan, a butter knife, a toaster) until he learns. - **Ask before using** your specialty items (e.g., "Can I use your cast iron for this?"). - **Clean up after himself** (no "granite is indestructible" logic). 5. **The Underlying Issue: Respect (or Lack Thereof)** - This isn’t just about kitchen rules—it’s about **how he treats shared spaces and your boundaries**. If he can’t respect your property, will he respect other things (your time, your feelings, your autonomy)? That’s a red flag for a healthy dynamic. - His reaction ("banishing me from my own house?") reveals a **power struggle**. You’re not "banishing" him—you’re **setting a boundary** to protect your things. If he can’t accept that, it’s a sign he may not respect your needs in other areas either. ### **What You Could Do Next:** - **Frame it as a team effort:** *"I love that you want to cook! But these tools are special to me, and I need to protect them. Let’s find a way for you to practice without damaging them—maybe I’ll get you a cheap pan to start with?"* - **Document the damage:** Take photos/videos of warped pans, stained counters, etc., as proof if he later claims it’s "not that bad." - **Consider a "cooking probation" period:** For a month, he only cooks with **his own** basic tools (no your knives, pans, or oven). If he proves he can handle them, you can revisit access. - **Address the yelling:** If he shouts when you correct him, that’s **disrespectful**. Say: *"I don’t yell at you when you make mistakes, so I’d appreciate it if you didn’t yell at me."* Boundaries matter. ### **When It’s Not Justified:** - If you’re **overreacting** (e.g., he’s a *great* cook but occasionally forgets to wipe the counter—this is different). - If you’re **withholding access permanently** without giving him a chance to change (unless he’s shown no remorse). - If you’re **using this as leverage** (e.g., "I’ll lock up the kitchen unless you do X other thing"). ### **Final Thought:** You’re not being unreasonable. You’re **protecting your property and your peace**. If he can’t respect that, it’s a sign of how he’ll treat other things in your life. A partner should **adapt to your needs**, not expect you to adapt to his carelessness. Would you like help drafting a script for how to talk to him about this? Or strategies for if he continues to resist?
